references.text: The same instruction regarding the fat is repeated for the peace offering of small livestock, emphasizing that the fat covering the entrails shall be offered as a fire offering to the Lord.
For the sin offering, the fat covering the entrails and all the fat on the entrails must be removed and offered, following the same principle as in the peace offering.
A detailed description of which parts of the fat are to be offered with the thank offering, including the fat that covers the entrails.
At the consecration of priests, the fat covering the entrails was to be burned on the altar, following the same practice as with the peace offering.
Prohibition against eating fat from animals that may be offered to the Lord, because the fat belongs to the Lord as a fire offering.
The priest shall sprinkle the blood and burn the fat as a pleasing aroma to the Lord, as described in the peace offering instruction.
Demonstrates that the requirement to remove the fat applies to both the peace offering and the sin offering, underscoring the central role of the sacrifice in atonement.
Uses the ritual of the peace offering as the standard for the sin offering, thereby linking the two forms of sacrifice theologically.
Confirms that the principle of removing the fat from the peace offering is the established standard for all other types of sacrifices.
Explains the theological reason (God's ownership) behind the ritual action described in the source verse.
Emphasizes that the ritual from the peace offering (the lamb) is the prevailing norm for handling the fat in other sacrifices.
